name: Willem, Chtholly and Seniorious
description: — Willem... — What's the matter? — It seems that there's something wrong with Seniorious... — I'll have a look... Seniorious is made by linking special talismans in particular order. After over 500 years, the carillon is now in bad condition, so Willem decides to examine it thoroughly. Seniorious has n pieces of talisman. Willem puts them in a line, the i -th of which is an integer a i . In order to maintain it, Willem needs to perform m operations. There are four types of operations: 1 l r x : For each i such that l ≤ i ≤ r , assign a i + x to a i . 2 l r x : For each i such that l ≤ i ≤ r , assign x to a i . 3 l r x : Print the x -th smallest number in the index range [ l , r ] , i.e. the element at the x -th position if all the elements a i such that l ≤ i ≤ r are taken and sorted into an array of non-decreasing integers. It's guaranteed that 1 ≤ x ≤ r - l + 1 . 4 l r x y : Print the sum of the x -th power of a i such that l ≤ i ≤ r , modulo y , i.e. .
input_specification: The only line contains four integers n , m , seed , v max ( 1 ≤ n , m ≤ 10 5 , 0 ≤ seed < 10 9 + 7, 1 ≤ vmax ≤ 10 9 ). The initial values and operations are generated using following pseudo code: def rnd(): ret = seed seed = (seed * 7 + 13) mod 1000000007 return ret for i = 1 to n: a[i] = (rnd() mod vmax) + 1 for i = 1 to m: op = (rnd() mod 4) + 1 l = (rnd() mod n) + 1 r = (rnd() mod n) + 1 if (l > r): swap(l, r) if (op == 3): x = (rnd() mod (r - l + 1)) + 1 else: x = (rnd() mod vmax) + 1 if (op == 4): y = (rnd() mod vmax) + 1 Here op is the type of the operation mentioned in the legend.
output_specification: For each operation of types 3 or 4 , output a line containing the answer.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 896C — Willem, Chtholly and Seniorious [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
